Module 2›Chapter 2.4›The Fabric Test Network
Core Concept

The Fabric Test Network

Your Sandbox for Hyperledger Fabric

The test-network is a pre-configured, simplified Hyperledger Fabric network provided within the fabric-samples repository. It's designed for developers to learn and experiment with Fabric's core functionalities in a controlled environment.

Why it matters

It provides a safe, isolated environment to practice network setup, chaincode deployment, and transaction execution without complex configurations.

Key Features
  • Demonstrates multi-organization interactions.
  • Supports channel creation and chaincode deployment.
  • Robust enough for core concept exploration.
Key Takeaway

The test-network is an indispensable tool for hands-on learning and rapid development in Hyperledger Fabric.

Pre-configured Environment

Ready-to-use setup for immediate experimentation.

Core Concepts Demonstrated

Channels, chaincode, organizations, and peers in action.

Simplified Learning Curve

Focus on blockchain logic, not complex infrastructure setup.

screens.title: Components of the Test Network
screens.narratorSegment: The test-network is composed of several key components, each playing a vital role in the network's operation. At its heart is the Ordering Service, which ensures that transactions are delivered to peers in a consistent and agreed-upon order. In our test-network, this is typically a single Raft-based orderer node, providing a practical example of a consensus mechanism. We also have Two Organizations, Org1 and Org2, simulating distinct business entities that wish to transact on the blockchain. Each organization is equipped with at least one Peer Node, which maintains a copy of the ledger and endorses transactions according to chaincode logic. Finally, Certificate Authorities (CAs) are crucial for issuing cryptographic identities to all network participants, ensuring secure and authenticated interactions. Understanding these components is like knowing the parts of an engine; it helps you comprehend how the entire system functions and where to look if issues arise. For instance, if transactions aren't being ordered, you'd investigate the Ordering Service. Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Components of the Test Network
Network Architecture

Components of the Test Network

Understanding the Building Blocks

Ordering Service

Ensures transaction order.

Two Organizations

Org1 & Org2 for transactions.

Peer Node per Org

Maintains ledger, endorses transactions.

Certificate Authorities

Issues cryptographic identities.

Component Roles
  • Ordering Service: Guarantees consistent transaction ordering across the network.
  • Organizations (Org1, Org2): Represent distinct business entities participating in the network.
  • Peer Nodes: Store the ledger and execute chaincode, endorsing transactions.
  • Certificate Authorities: Provide digital identities for secure authentication and authorization.
Real-world Analogy

Think of the `test-network` as a small, self-contained company with two departments (Org1, Org2). The Ordering Service is like the company's internal mailroom, ensuring all documents are processed in order. Each department has a records office (Peer Node) to keep copies of all transactions, and an HR department (CA) to issue employee IDs.

Key Takeaway

Each component plays a specific, interdependent role in maintaining the integrity and functionality of the Fabric network.

Module 2›Chapter 2.4›The network.sh Control Script
Network Management

The network.sh Control Script

Orchestrating Your Fabric Environment

The network.sh script, located in fabric-samples/test-network, is a powerful shell script designed to simplify the management of your Hyperledger Fabric test-network. It automates many complex, multi-step operations.

Key Functions
  • Bring up the network (up)
  • Create channels (createChannel)
  • Deploy chaincode (deployCC)
  • Shut down and clean up (down)
Benefit

It abstracts away the complexities of manual Docker commands and cryptographic tool execution, saving significant time and reducing errors.

Key Takeaway

network.sh is your essential command-line utility for efficient lifecycle management of the test-network.

Terminal: fabric-samples/test-network
$ ./network.sh --help
Usage:
  network.sh <Mode> [Flags]
  Modes:
    up             - Bring up the network
    down           - Tear down the network
    createChannel  - Create a channel
    deployCC       - Deploy chaincode
    ...
Flags:
  -c <channel name>  - Channel name
  -ccn <chaincode name> - Chaincode name
  -ccp <chaincode path> - Chaincode path
  -ccl <chaincode language> - Chaincode language

This output shows the various commands and flags available with network.sh, highlighting its versatility in managing the Fabric network lifecycle.

screens.title: Bringing Up the Test Network
screens.narratorSegment: The first step to interacting with your Fabric network is bringing it online using the. slash network. sh up command. When you execute this, a series of critical actions unfold. First, cryptogen is invoked to generate all the necessary cryptographic materials – certificates and keys – for each organization (Org1, Org2) and the ordering service. These identities are fundamental for secure communication and transaction signing. Next, configtxgen creates the genesis block for the ordering service, which is the very first block in the blockchain, and also generates the channel configuration transaction. Finally, docker-compose files are used to launch all the Docker containers for the Certificate Authorities, the orderer node, and the peer nodes for both organizations. This entire process sets up the foundational infrastructure. A common mistake here is not being in the correct fabric-samples slash test-network directory, leading to a "command not found" error. Always verify your current working directory before executing network. sh commands. Bringing Up the Test Network means the `./network.sh up` command generates cryptographic materials, creates configuration blocks, and starts docker containers for the fabric network.. In practical terms, initializing your fabric environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Bringing Up the Test Network
Network Lifecycle

Bringing Up the Test Network

Initializing Your Fabric Environment

Terminal: fabric-samples/test-network
$ ./network.sh up
Creating network with command 'up'
...
Creating Org1 CA ... Done
Creating Org2 CA ... Done
Creating Orderer ... Done
Creating Org1 peer ... Done
Creating Org2 peer ... Done
...
Network started successfully!

This output confirms the successful startup of all necessary Docker containers for the `test-network`.

Process Steps
  • Cryptographic Material Generation: `cryptogen` creates identities for organizations and the orderer.
  • Configuration Artifacts: `configtxgen` creates the genesis block and channel configuration.
  • Docker Container Launch: CAs, orderer, and peer nodes are started via `docker-compose`.
Common Mistake

Forgetting to navigate into the fabric-samples/test-network directory before running ./network.sh up will result in a "command not found" error.

Key Takeaway

./network.sh up orchestrates the entire initial setup, from crypto generation to container startup, establishing the network's foundation.

screens.title: Establishing a Communication Channel
screens.narratorSegment: Once your network is up and running, the next crucial step is to establish a channel. A channel in Hyperledger Fabric is essentially a private "subnet" or communication layer that allows specific organizations to transact confidentially. It ensures that only authorized participants can see and interact with the transactions and ledger data associated with that channel. To create a channel, you'll use the command. slash network. sh create Channel -c mychannel. This command performs two main actions: it first generates the necessary channel configuration artifact, which defines the channel's policies and participants. Then, it instructs the peer nodes of Org1 and Org2 to join this newly created channel. This process is vital because without a channel, organizations cannot communicate or share ledger data. A common misconception is that all organizations on a Fabric network automatically share all data; channels enforce the necessary privacy and data segregation required in multi-party business networks. Establishing a Communication Channel means channels provide a private, isolated communication and transaction layer between specific organizations in a fabric network.. In practical terms, private data exchange between organizations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Establishing a Communication Channel
Channel Configuration

Establishing a Communication Channel

Private Data Exchange Between Organizations

Terminal: fabric-samples/test-network
$ ./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel
Creating channel 'mychannel'
...
Channel 'mychannel' created successfully.
Peer0.org1 joined channel 'mychannel'.
Peer0.org2 joined channel 'mychannel'.

This output confirms the creation of 'mychannel' and that both Org1 and Org2 peers have successfully joined it.

What is a Channel?

A channel is a private communication layer that enables specific organizations to transact and share ledger data confidentially.

Command Actions
  • Generates the channel configuration artifact.
  • Instructs specified peer nodes (Org1, Org2) to join the new channel.
Misconception

Not all organizations on a Fabric network automatically share all data. Channels enforce necessary privacy and data segregation.

Key Takeaway

Channels are fundamental for privacy and controlled data sharing, defining who can see and interact with specific transactions.

screens.title: Deploying Chaincode to the Channel
screens.narratorSegment: With a channel established, you're ready to deploy chaincode, which are Hyperledger Fabric's smart contracts. Chaincode defines the business logic and rules for managing assets or data on the ledger. The fabric-samples repository includes various examples, such as asset-transfer-basic, which we'll use. To deploy it, you'll execute a command like. slash network. sh deploy CC -ccn basic -ccp.. slash asset-transfer-basic slash chaincode-go -ccl go. Let's break down these parameters: -ccn basic assigns a name to your chaincode, -ccp specifies the path to its source code, and -ccl indicates the programming language, in this case, Go. The deployment process itself is multi-stage: the chaincode is first installed on the relevant peers, then its definition is approved by each participating organization, and finally, the definition is committed to the channel. This ensures that all organizations agree on the exact version and rules of the smart contract before it becomes active. Incorrect paths or language specifications are common errors here, so double-check your command. Deploying Chaincode to the Channel means deploying chaincode involves installing, approving, and committing its definition to a channel, activating the smart contract logic.. In practical terms, bringing business logic to the ledger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Setting Up for Peer CLI Interaction
CLI Interaction

Setting Up for Peer CLI Interaction

Configuring Your Environment to Engage with Chaincode

Terminal: Configure for Org1 Peer0
$ export CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED=true
$ export CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID="Org1MSP"
$ export CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt
$ export CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/users/Admin@org1.example.com/msp
$ export CORE_PEER_ADDRESS=localhost:7051

These commands configure your shell environment to interact with `peer0.org1.example.com` securely.

Key Environment Variables
  • CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED: Enables secure (TLS) communication.
  • CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID: Identifies the local organization's MSP ID.
  • CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE: Path to the peer's TLS root certificate.
  • CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH: Path to the user's cryptographic identity.
  • CORE_PEER_ADDRESS: The endpoint of the target peer node.
Common Issue

Incorrectly set environment variables are a frequent cause of connection errors or permission denied messages when using the peer CLI.

Key Takeaway

Accurate environment variable configuration is crucial for the peer CLI to authenticate and communicate effectively with the network.

screens.title: Invoking Chaincode Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Once your environment variables are correctly set, you can perform an invoke operation on your chaincode. An invoke command is used to execute a function within your smart contract that modifies the state of the ledger. This means it creates, updates, or deletes data. For instance, to initialize the asset-transfer-basic chaincode with some initial assets, you would call its Init Ledger function. The peer chaincode invoke command requires several parameters, including the orderer's address, TLS certificates for secure communication, the channel name, the chaincode name, and importantly, the function to call along with any arguments in JSON format. This command triggers a transaction proposal, which is then endorsed by peers, ordered by the ordering service, and finally committed to the ledger. If the transaction is successful, the ledger state is updated across all participating peers. A common mistake is providing incorrect peer addresses or TLS root certificate files, which prevents the transaction from being properly endorsed or committed. content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Invoking Chaincode Functions
Ledger Operations

Invoking Chaincode Functions

Modifying the Ledger State with Transactions

Terminal: Invoke InitLedger
$ peer chaincode invoke -o localhost:7050 \
  --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls \
  --cafile ${PWD}/organizations/ordererOrganizations/example.com/orderers/orderer.example.com/msp/tlscacerts/tlsca.example.com-cert.pem \
  -C mychannel -n basic \
  --peerAddresses localhost:7051 --tlsRootCertFiles ${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt \
  --peerAddresses localhost:9051 --tlsRootCertFiles ${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org2.example.com/peers/peer0.org2.example.com/tls/ca.crt \
  -c '{"function":"InitLedger","Args":[]}'
...
2023-10-26 10:30:45.123 UTC [chaincodeCmd] chaincodeInvokeOrQuery -> INFO 001 Chaincode invoke successful. result: status:200

This command initializes the ledger by calling the `InitLedger` function of the `basic` chaincode.

Invoke Purpose

Executes a chaincode function that modifies the ledger state (e.g., creating, updating, or deleting assets).

Key Parameters
  • -o: Orderer address.
  • --tls, --cafile: TLS configuration for secure communication.
  • -C: Channel name.
  • -n: Chaincode name.
  • -c: JSON payload specifying function and arguments.
Troubleshooting Tip

Ensure all --peerAddresses and --tlsRootCertFiles are correct for all endorsing peers to avoid transaction failures.

Key Takeaway

Invoke commands are the primary way to interact with and update the shared, immutable ledger in Hyperledger Fabric.

screens.title: Querying the Ledger State
screens.narratorSegment: In contrast to an invoke operation, a query operation allows you to read the current state of the ledger without making any modifications. This is a read-only transaction, meaning it doesn't go through the full consensus process of an invoke; it's typically executed directly against a single peer. To retrieve all assets from our asset-transfer-basic chaincode, you would use the peer chaincode query command, specifying the channel name, chaincode name, and the Get All Assets function. The result will be a JSON array containing the current data stored on the ledger. Querying is fundamental for any application built on Fabric, as it provides the means to retrieve and display the blockchain's current state to users. It's important to remember that a query only reflects the state on the peer it's executed against, which should be consistent across all peers on the channel due to the ledger's immutability and replication. If you see inconsistent results, it might indicate a synchronization issue or a problem with the peer's ledger. Querying the Ledger State means a query operation retrieves data from the ledger without altering its state, providing read-only access to the blockchain.. In practical terms, reading data without modification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Querying the Ledger State
Ledger Operations

Querying the Ledger State

Reading Data Without Modification

Terminal: Query All Assets
$ peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'
[{"ID":"asset1","color":"blue","size":5,"owner":"Tomoko","appraisedValue":300},
 {"ID":"asset2","color":"red","size":5,"owner":"Brad","appraisedValue":400},
 {"ID":"asset3","color":"green","size":10,"owner":"Jin","appraisedValue":500},
 {"ID":"asset4","color":"yellow","size":10,"owner":"Aarav","appraisedValue":600},
 {"ID":"asset5","color":"black","size":15,"owner":"Pari","appraisedValue":700},
 {"ID":"asset6","color":"white","size":15,"owner":"Valeria","appraisedValue":800}]

This output shows a JSON array of assets, representing the current state of the ledger.

Query Purpose

Reads data from the ledger without initiating a transaction or modifying the state. It's a read-only operation.

Key Parameters
  • -C: Channel name.
  • -n: Chaincode name.
  • -c: JSON payload specifying the function and arguments (e.g., GetAllAssets).
Consistency Check

While queries are typically against a single peer, the ledger's immutability ensures consistency across all peers on the channel. Inconsistent results may indicate a synchronization issue.

Key Takeaway

Query operations are essential for retrieving and displaying the current state of the blockchain to users without altering the ledger.

Module 2›Chapter 2.4›Shutting Down and Cleaning Up
Network Maintenance

Shutting Down and Cleaning Up

Ensuring a Fresh Start for Your Environment

Terminal: Shut Down Network
$ ./network.sh down
Tearing down network with command 'down'
...
Removing Org1 CA ... Done
Removing Org2 CA ... Done
Removing Orderer ... Done
Removing Org1 peer ... Done
Removing Org2 peer ... Done
Removing generated crypto material and config artifacts ... Done
Network torn down successfully!

This output confirms the complete shutdown and removal of all network components and artifacts.

Cleanup Actions
  • Stops and removes all Docker containers (CAs, orderers, peers).
  • Deletes generated cryptographic material (certificates, keys).
  • Removes configuration artifacts and chaincode images.
Why Cleanup is Important

Frees up system resources, prevents conflicts with future deployments, and ensures a clean slate for consistent development and testing.

Troubleshooting Tip

Always read terminal output carefully; Fabric provides detailed error messages that can guide your troubleshooting efforts.

Key Takeaway

Regular cleanup with ./network.sh down is crucial for maintaining a healthy and predictable development environment.

The first step to interacting with your Fabric network is bringing it online using the. slash network. sh up command. When you execute this, a series of critical actions unfold. Once your network is up and running, the next crucial step is to establish a channel. A channel in Hyperledger Fabric is essentially a private "subnet" or communication layer that allows specific organizations to transact confidentially. It ensures that only authorized participants can see and interact with the transactions and ledger data associated with that channel. To create a channel, you'll use the command. slash network. sh create Channel -c mychannel. This command performs two main actions: it first generates the necessary channel configuration artifact, which defines the channel's policies and participants. Then, it instructs the peer nodes of Org1 and Org2 to join this newly created channel. This process is vital because without a channel, organizations cannot communicate or share ledger data. A common misconception is that all organizations on a Fabric network automatically share all data; channels enforce the necessary privacy and data segregation required in multi-party business networks. In contrast to an invoke operation, a query operation allows you to read the current state of the ledger without making any modifications. This is a read-only transaction, meaning it doesn't go through the full consensus process of an invoke; it's typically executed directly against a single peer. Let's recap some essential concepts from this chapter. The test-network is a pre-configured sample Hyperledger Fabric network, ideal for development and learning, found within fabric-samples. It provides a safe, isolated environment to experiment with blockchain functionalities. The Ordering Service is a critical component responsible for establishing a total order of transactions across the network, ensuring consistency among all participants. A Peer Node is where the ledger is maintained and transactions are endorsed, acting as the primary interface for applications. The Certificate Authority (CA) is vital for issuing and managing cryptographic identities, ensuring secure and authenticated interactions within the network. Finally, a Channel serves as a private communication layer, enabling specific organizations to conduct confidential transactions and maintain separate ledgers. These components collectively form the backbone of any functional Fabric network.

Continuing our review, Chaincode refers to the smart contracts that define the business logic and rules for managing the ledger state, essentially the "programs" that run on your blockchain. The network. sh script is the primary command-line tool within the test-network directory, used for managing the entire network lifecycle, from bringing it up to tearing it down. The peer CLI is the command-line interface that developers use to interact directly with peer nodes and chaincode, allowing for administrative tasks and transaction execution. An Invoke operation is a type of transaction that modifies the ledger state, such as creating or updating an asset. In contrast, a Query operation is a read-only transaction that retrieves data from the ledger without altering its state. Mastering these tools and operations is fundamental for building and managing decentralized applications on Hyperledger Fabric.
